# Abstract

The three centuries spanning the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate under Qutb al-Din Aibak in 1206AD to the First Battle of Panipat in 1526AD witnessed profound structural transformations across the Indian subcontinent. Across an aggregate domain of 3,94M km² (encompassing 3.938.787 km² and 51.246 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells), regional population expanded from 74M inhabitants in 1206AD to 81M in 1300AD, 83M in 1350AD, 86,5M in 1400AD, 91M in 1450AD and 97M by 1526AD. This secular expansion increased aggregate demographic density from 18,79 to 24,63 persons per km², propelled by the intensification of double-cropped agriculture, hydraulic canal engineering in the Indo-Gangetic alluvium, the systematic fiscal conversion of tributary agrarian obligations into monetised iqta revenue demands, and the rapid expansion of nucleated urban centres and rural market towns (qasbahs).

Reconstructed across five macro-regions under INDUS, regional demographic weight remained firmly anchored in the alluvial plains of northern and eastern India. The Delhi Core, Upper Doab, Awadh and Jaunpur division expanded from 20,72M inhabitants in 1206AD to 27,16M in 1526AD, attaining an average density of 50,79 persons per km² across 534.801 km² of fertile riverine floodplains. Concurrently, the Bengal Sultanate, Bihar, Gajapati Orissa and Assam division grew from 18,5M to 24,25M across 803.833 km² (density rising from 23,01 to 30,17 persons per km²), reflecting the agrarian opening of the eastern deltaic frontiers and lucrative maritime commerce across the Bay of Bengal. In western and central India, the Gujarat and Malwa sultanates together with the Rajput confederacies increased from 14,06M to 18,43M across 975.022 km², sustained by Persian Gulf and Arabian Sea textile trade radiating through Cambay, Surat and Broach. In the peninsular south, the Bahmani Sultanate and its five successor sultanates mirrored this expansion, rising from 14,06M to 18,43M across 777.163 km² (density increasing from 18,09 to 23,71 persons per km²), while the north-western frontier of Lahore, Multan and Samma Sindh supported 6,66M to 8,73M across 847.968 km² of arid and semi-arid riverine tracts.

This study integrates 34.677 catalogued settlements with chronological population series, reconciling 35.477 source-ledger candidates against Persian chronicles, Sultanate and early Mughal fiscal registers, colonial gazetteers, epigraphic corpora, numismatic distributions and regional archaeological surveys [@Habib1982Atlas; @Moosvi1987Economy; @ImperialGazetteer1908]. By subtracting nucleated urban centres directly from regional demographic totals at each benchmark, the reconstruction isolates genuine urban agglomeration from surrounding rural densities. The resulting spatial synthesis provides a grounded baseline for mediaeval Indian demographic history, documenting how institutional innovations under the Mamluk, Khalji and Tughlaq dynasties, followed by the flourishing of autonomous regional successor states in Bengal, Gujarat, Jaunpur and the Deccan, reshaped the settlement geography of South Asia prior to the Mughal conquest.

# Historical Demography and Regional Partition

## Agrarian Systems and the Iqta Extraction Framework

The institutional foundation of mediaeval Indian demographic growth was the establishment of the iqta system, which replaced earlier fragmented feudal land-grant mechanisms with centralised, transferable revenue assignments [@Singh2023Paradigm; @Eaton2019India]. Under the Mamluk and Khalji sultans, the state asserted sovereign ownership over agricultural surplus, granting military commanders (muqtis or walis) the right to collect land revenue (kharaj) and poll tax (jizya) from designated administrative territories [@Aamir2026Slave; @Malik2026Trade].

Because iqta holders were frequently rotated between provinces to prevent the consolidation of hereditary territorial power bases, surplus extraction was systematically channelled into provincial and imperial capitals rather than dissipated in isolated rural manors [@Ali2023Historical; @Eaton2019India]. This administrative mobility discouraged local entrenched warlordism and created a unified fiscal conduit between rural producers and metropolitan consumers.

Crucially, the Sultanate fiscal regime required peasants to discharge a substantial fraction of their revenue dues in cash rather than kind, particularly following the comprehensive agrarian reforms of Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296AD-1316AD) [@Malik2026Trade]. This fiscal mechanism forced rural cultivators to bring grain, pulses, cotton and oilseeds to designated market towns (mandis and qasbahs), catalysing rural monetisation and stimulating commercial interregional trade [@Sheikh2021Persian; @Guha2011Forms].

Local village headmen (muqaddams and chaudhuris) and rural accountants (patwaris) were integrated into a hierarchical accounting apparatus, bridging the institutional gap between vernacular agrarian villages and the Persianate administrative elite [@Sheikh2021Persian; @Eaton2019India]. Village records kept in local vernaculars were audited against imperial registers in Persian, establishing an administrative paper trail that survived dynastic upheavals [@Sheikh2021Persian].

The demographic consequence of this fiscal extraction was rapid urbanisation. Surplus grain collected from the hinterlands supported dense non-agricultural populations in royal capitals, provincial garrison citadels, textile weaving centres and transit river ports [@Malik2026Trade; @Bhandral2023Analyzing]. Craftsmen, stonecutters, ironmongers, leatherworkers and weavers congregated in emerging urban centres, incentivised by high urban demand and the patronage of Sultanate elites [@Mahata2024Distinctiv; @BurtonPage2008Documentat].

Furthermore, the expansion of the iqta system incentivised the clearing of virgin forests and the reclamation of waste lands [@Amir2023Taking; @Khan2024Hydraulic]. Sultans and governors frequently offered concessionary tax rates (in'am and madad-i ma'ash) to religious scholars, Sufi shaykhs and military veterans who established new settlements in frontier tracts, transforming scrub jungles into productive agricultural landscapes [@Hannan2025Sufic; @Malik2021Colonial].

The monetisation of agrarian tribute also spurred the development of sophisticated merchant banking instruments [@Guha2011Forms; @Sheikh2021Persian]. Indigenous bankers (sarrafs) issued bills of exchange (hundis) that permitted merchants and revenue collectors to transfer vast sums of money across hundreds of leagues without transporting physical specie along perilous highway routes [@Guha2011Forms]. This commercial credit infrastructure lowered the cost of moving food grains and raw cotton to processing centres, lubricating interprovincial trade between the agricultural hinterlands and metropolitan bazaars [@Malik2026Trade; @Naqvi1968Urbanisation].

## Five Administrative Macro-Regions

INDUS partitions the territory of the Delhi Sultanate and its successor states into five physiographically and administratively coherent macro-regions (Table \ref{tab:subregions}):

### Delhi Core, Upper Doab, Awadh and Jaunpur Sultanate

The Delhi Core, Upper Doab, Awadh and Jaunpur Sultanate macro-region (534.801 km², 13,58% of regional area) spans the upper and middle Gangetic alluvium between the Himalayas and the Vindhyan foothills [@Khan2024Hydraulic; @Vashishta2026Geography]. Endowed with deep alluvial soils and reliable rainfall supplemented by perennial Himalayan tributaries, this division formed the political and economic core of northern India.

The imperial capital shifted through a succession of fortified foundations in the Delhi triangle: Qila Rai Pithora, Siri, Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, Firozabad and subsequently Agra under Sikandar Lodi [@BurtonPage2008Documentat; @Mahata2024Distinctiv]. Each successive royal city represented an ambitious demographic nucleation, drawing tens of thousands of soldiers, builders, scholars and merchants within extensive stone and rubble ramparts [@Mahata2024Distinctiv].

Following the devastation wrought by Timur's invasion in 1398AD, the Sharqi dynasty established the Jaunpur Sultanate along the Gomti River, patronising magnificent architectural monuments and creating an independent regional centre of Islamic jurisprudence and learning [@Joshi2026Sacred; @Kulke2009Bibliograp; @Bayly1983Rulers]. Population climbed from 20,72M in 1206AD to 27,16M in 1526AD across 5.362 catalogued settlements, maintaining the highest demographic density on the subcontinent at 50,79 persons per km².

The Doab and Awadh plains sustained high agricultural productivity through intensive crop rotation combining wheat and barley in the spring harvest with rice, millets and sugarcane in the autumn harvest [@Khan2024Hydraulic; @Habib1982Atlas]. The region was crisscrossed by arterial river routes on the Ganga and Yamuna, facilitating large-scale grain flotillas that supplied the metropolitan markets of Delhi, Kannauj and Jaunpur, while upland Newar urban polities in the Kathmandu valley linked trans-Himalayan trade to the Gangetic rim [@Slusser1982NepalMandala].

### Bengal Sultanate, Bihar, Gajapati Orissa and Assam

The Bengal Sultanate, Bihar, Gajapati Orissa and Assam macro-region (803.833 km², 20,41%) encompasses the lower Gangetic basin, the deltaic wetlands of Bengal, the Brahmaputra valley of Assam and the coastal maritime plains of Orissa, containing 8.389 catalogued settlements [@Salim2026Social; @Kulke2009Bibliograp; @Eaton1993Rise].

The Bengal Sultanate, achieving autonomy from Delhi under the Ilyas Shahi and Husain Shahi dynasties, integrated rich wet-rice agriculture with international maritime trade across the Indian Ocean [@Eaton1993Rise; @Eaton2019India; @Salim2026Social]. Monumental brick capitals flourished at Gaur (Lakhnauti) and Pandua, while Sonargaon and Chittagong functioned as flourishing riverine and maritime emporia.

Sufi khanqahs and pioneer communities played an active role in clearing the dense mangrove and riverine forests of the eastern delta, bringing vast new alluvial tracts under wet-rice cultivation [@Eaton1993Rise; @Eaton2019India; @Salim2026Social]. This eastern agrarian frontier generated immense food surpluses that supported both high rural densities and prosperous commercial ports trading fine muslins, silk and rice with Southeast Asia and China [@Salim2026Social].

Riverine mobility in Bengal was sustained by massive flotillas of transport cargo barges and armed war-boats (nawwara) operating along the complex anastomosing channels of the Padma, Meghna and Brahmaputra [@Salim2026Social; @Eaton2019India]. These amphibious networks allowed the sultans of Bengal to project political power across seasonally flooded deltaic terrains that resisted conventional cavalry tactics, ensuring uninterrupted grain transport from agrarian reclamation zones to the metropolitan storage granaries of Gaur and Pandua, while foothills along the northern Assam frontier bordered Bhutanese monastic polities [@Eaton1993Rise; @Phuntsho2013HistoryBhutan].

In the south, the Hindu Gajapati kingdom of Orissa commanded the Mahanadi delta and coastal littoral from its fortified seat at Cuttack (Barabati fort), combining hydraulic temple complexes such as Puri with fortified frontiers resisting both Bahmani and Bengal sultanate incursions [@Kulke2009Bibliograp; @Jha2025Geoarchaeo]. Sub-regional population rose from 18,5M in 1206AD to 24,25M in 1526AD (30,17 persons per km²).

### Gujarat Sultanate, Malwa Sultanate and Rajput States

The Gujarat Sultanate, Malwa Sultanate and Rajput States macro-region (975.022 km², 24,75%) encompasses the arid western desert fringe of Rajasthan, the black-soil agricultural tracts of the Malwa plateau and the maritime coast of Gujarat, spanning 5.708 catalogued settlements [@Sheikh2004State; @Amir2023Taking; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making].

Independent under the Muzaffarid dynasty after 1407AD, the Gujarat Sultanate emerged as a pre-eminent commercial powerhouse, anchored on the new capital of Ahmedabad founded in 1411AD and the international ports of Cambay (Khambhat), Surat, Broach and Diu [@Sheikh2004State; @Sheikh2021Persian]. Merchants from Cairo, Hormuz, Aden and Malacca traded actively in Gujarati emporia, exchanging horses, bullion and spices for cotton fabrics, indigo and silks [@Sheikh2004State].

Industrial craft specialisation in Gujarat supported dense peri-urban manufacturing belts [@Sheikh2004State; @Sheikh2021Persian]. Extensive indigo plantations surrounding Sarkhej and Bayana supplied brilliant blue dyes for export textiles, while local shipyards along the Gulf of Khambhat utilised durable Malabar teak to construct ocean-going dhows capable of navigating monsoon routes to East Africa and the Indonesian archipelago [@Sheikh2004State]. In the inland city of Patan, master weavers produced double-ikat patola silks prized across Asian royal courts [@Sheikh2004State].

To the east, the Malwa Sultanate, ruled by the Khalji and Ghurid dynasties from the lofty plateau fortress of Mandu (Shadiabad), controlled vital transit corridors crossing the Vindhyan range [@BurtonPage2008Documentat]. Perched on an isolated tableland surrounded by sheer sandstone cliffs, Mandu housed elaborate palace compounds, immense grain storage silos and extensive rainwater collection reservoirs [@BurtonPage2008Documentat].

In the arid and semi-arid interior, Rajput clan confederacies in Mewar (Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh) and Marwar (Jodhpur, Nagaur) developed fortified hilltop settlements and extensive stepwell networks, balancing agrarian grazing with military service [@Amir2023Taking; @Singh2023Paradigm]. Population grew from 14,06M in 1206AD to 18,43M in 1526AD (18,9 persons per km²).

### Bahmani and Deccan Sultanates

The Bahmani and Deccan Sultanates macro-region (777.163 km², 19,73%) encompasses the basaltic Deccan lava trap and granitic plateaus of Maharashtra, northern Karnataka and Telangana, recording 8.125 catalogued settlements [@Eaton2019India; @Chatterjee2006Slavery; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade].

Founded in 1347AD by Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah in revolt against Muhammad bin Tughlaq, the Bahmani Sultanate established successive imperial capitals at Gulbarga (Ahsanabad) and Bidar (Muhammadabad), integrating Persianate military elites, Central Asian horse merchants and indigenous Deccani elites [@BurtonPage2008Documentat; @Torri2014Periodizat]. In the late fifteenth century, the Bahmani polity fractured into five autonomous Deccan Sultanates: Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Golconda (Qutb Shahi), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi) and Bidar (Barid Shahi).

Across this rugged plateau terrain, population expanded from 14,06M in 1206AD to 18,43M in 1526AD (23,71 persons per km²), sustained by dryland millet, sorghum and cotton farming, alongside international diamond mining in Golconda. The region maintained active maritime connections through west-coast ports such as Chaul, Dabhol and Goa, importing thousands of warhorses annually from the Persian Gulf to sustain Deccani cavalry forces [@Chatterjee2006Slavery; @Eaton2019India].

Major fortified citadels at Daulatabad, Golconda, Parenda and Naldurg featured advanced military architecture, including deep moats cut into solid basalt, concentric curtain walls and ingenious mechanical sally ports that protected administrative populations during protracted sieges [@BurtonPage2008Documentat].

Military recruitment and demographic vitality in the Deccan were inextricably tied to trans-oceanic cavalry logistics [@Chatterjee2006Slavery; @Eaton2019India]. Because high humidity and endemic parasitic diseases in peninsular India prevented the successful domestic breeding of heavy warhorses, Deccan rulers maintained royal monopolies over the importation of Arabian and Persian mounts through west-coast anchorages such as Chaul, Dabhol and Bhatkal [@Eaton2019India]. The substantial revenues generated by the diamond mines of Kollur and Golconda funded these lavish equine importations, which in turn sustained the military supremacy of urban-based garrison elites over surrounding rural peasantries [@Chatterjee2006Slavery; @Eaton2019India].

### Lahore, Multan and Samma Sindh Frontier

The Lahore, Multan and Samma Sindh Frontier macro-region (847.968 km², 21,53%) comprises the alluvial floodplains of the five Punjab rivers, the Salt Range, the Peshawar basin and the lower Indus valley of Sindh, encompassing 7.093 catalogued settlements rooted in long-lived Indus alluvial corridors [@Ali2023Historical; @Malik2021Colonial; @Possehl1999IndusAge; @Kenoyer1998AncientCities].

Throughout the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, this region operated as a militarised frontier bastion shielding the Delhi Sultanate against continuous Mongol invasions from Central Asia [@Ali2023Historical; @Hannan2025Sufic]. Garrison forts at Dipalpur, Samana, Sunam and Multan were heavily garrisoned by seasoned marcher lords, such as Ghazi Malik (the future Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq), who repelled repeated incursions by the Chagatai Khanate [@Ali2023Historical].

Multan flourished as an indispensable spiritual and commercial crossroads, anchored by influential Suhrawardi Sufi establishments [@Hannan2025Sufic; @Malik2021Colonial]. The shrines of Baha al-Din Zakariya and Rukn-i-Alam served as pilgrimage centres and diplomatic intermediaries, mediating between Sultanate governors and local pastoral tribes [@Hannan2025Sufic].

In lower Sindh, the indigenous Samma dynasty ruled from Thatta and the Makli necropolis, controlling Arabian Sea trade and irrigated flood-basin agriculture along the Indus delta [@Ali2023Historical]. Sub-regional population grew from 6,66M in 1206AD to 8,73M in 1526AD (10,3 persons per km²).

The frontier landscape was further shaped by autonomous tribal groups in the Salt Range and Potohar plateau [@Ali2023Historical; @Malik2021Colonial]. Communities such as the Gakhars and Khokhars controlled key river defiles and transit passes across the Jhelum and Indus, extracting tolls from passing merchant caravans and frequently clashing with Sultanate garrison commanders [@Ali2023Historical]. Secure transit along the overland trade routes connecting Multan and Lahore through the Bolan and Gomal passes to Qandahar required delicate political negotiations and formal subsidy payments to local pastoral chieftains [@Malik2021Colonial].

# Agrarian Technologies, Canal Engineering and Urbanisation

## Hydraulic Infrastructure and Canal Irrigation

The steady demographic expansion of mediaeval India was supported by substantial technological advances in agricultural hydraulics and irrigation engineering [@GANI2026Canal; @Khan2024Hydraulic]. Prior to the fourteenth century, irrigation in northern India relied primarily on monsoon rains, seasonal inundation canals, masonry tanks and manual leather-bucket well lifting. Under the Tughlaq dynasty, imperial state policy shifted towards large-scale hydraulic infrastructure construction to stabilise agricultural yields against recurring drought [@GANI2026Canal; @Khan2024Hydraulic].

Firoz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351AD-1388AD) instituted the most extensive canal construction programme in pre-modern South Asian history [@GANI2026Canal; @Vashishta2026Geography]. The Rajbaha and Ulughkhani canals tapped the waters of the Yamuna and Satluj rivers, carrying perennial irrigation flows across more than two hundred kilometres of arid terrain into the eastern Punjab and Haryana plains [@GANI2026Canal].

This hydraulic network brought thousands of hectares of previously fallow scrubland under permanent multi-cropping, supporting the foundation of new urban centres such as Hissar Firoza and Fatehabad [@Vashishta2026Geography]. State canals enabled the widespread double-cropping of high-value cash crops, including sugarcane, wheat, oilseeds and indigo, substantially enhancing caloric and economic output per unit area [@Khan2024Hydraulic; @Malik2026Trade].

Complementing major riverine canals, mechanical water-lifting devices diffused widely across the subcontinent during this era [@Bhandral2023Analyzing; @Amir2023Taking]. The introduction and dissemination of the geared Persian wheel (saqiya), fitted with pinions and earthen pot chains driven by bullock power, transformed well irrigation throughout the Punjab, Rajasthan and Gujarat [@Bhandral2023Analyzing].

By enabling continuous water extraction from deep water tables, the saqiya allowed intensive garden cultivation and rabi (winter) grain production in semi-arid zones. In the Deccan and western India, rulers and merchant guilds constructed elaborate stepwells (baolis) and masonry water reservoirs, providing municipal drinking water for urban populations while recharging surrounding agricultural aquifers [@Amir2023Taking; @BurtonPage2008Documentat].

## Monetisation, Grain Markets and Settlement Expansion

Urbanisation in the Sultanate period was closely linked to market regulation and monetary policy [@Malik2026Trade; @Sheikh2021Persian]. Alauddin Khalji introduced rigorous price-control regulations across northern India, fixing statutory ceiling prices for food grains, textiles, horses and draught animals [@Malik2026Trade].

To maintain stable provisions for the massive imperial army stationed at Delhi, the state established imperial granaries and mandated that half the land revenue in the Doab be paid directly in grain [@Malik2026Trade; @Eaton2019India]. Hoarding was severely penalised, and transport merchants (karwanis or banjaras) were registered with the state, ensuring that harvested crops moved swiftly from rural threshing floors to urban storage depots [@Malik2026Trade].

Underpinning these commercial networks was a uniform, bimetallic coinage system initiated by Iltutmish, based on the silver tanka (approximately 175 grains) and copper jital [@Malik2026Trade; @Eaton2019India]. This reliable currency circulated widely from Multan to Bengal, lowering transaction costs and facilitating extensive credit mechanisms operated by sarrafs (money changers and bankers) [@Sheikh2021Persian; @Guha2011Forms].

Even when Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experimental introduction of token copper and brass currency (1329AD-1332AD) collapsed due to widespread counterfeiting, the underlying silver and copper standards recovered swiftly under subsequent rulers [@Eaton2019India; @Malik2026Trade]. Mints established across provincial capitals, including Lakhnauti, Sonargaon, Daulatabad and Ahmedabad, supported high-velocity regional exchange and facilitated the payment of wages to building artisans and textile workers [@Sheikh2004State; @Salim2026Social].

Monetary circulation stimulated non-agricultural craft production across provincial towns. The adoption of the spinning wheel (charkha) in the thirteenth century dramatically reduced the labour hours required to produce cotton yarn, fostering a textile revolution that made Indian cotton cloths the premier export across the Indian Ocean basin [@Malik2026Trade].

Paper manufacturing, sericulture, iron casting and lime-mortar masonry similarly diffused throughout provincial urban centres, encouraging skilled artisan immigration and reinforcing the growth of secondary administrative hubs and manufacturing centres [@Mahata2024Distinctiv; @BurtonPage2008Documentat]. The use of lime mortar enabled the construction of wide-spanning domes and true arches, accelerating the erection of multi-storey urban buildings, caravanserais and defensive battlements [@Mahata2024Distinctiv].

# Methodological Framework and Spatial Calibration

## Raster Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To distribute population across 3.938.787 km² of terrestrial surface, the INDUS spatial engine partitions the subcontinent into 51.246 active 5-arcminute grid cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes). Each terrestrial pixel is evaluated against four primary environmental and historical covariates:

1. Fluvial proximity and hydrological drainage: distance decay towards perennial river systems (Ganga, Yamuna, Indus, Brahmaputra, Narmada, Tapi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery), with density weights attenuating exponentially beyond 20 km from reliable surface water.
2. Topographic slope and elevation penalties: steep escarpments exceeding 15% slope across the Himalayan foothills, Western Ghats and Aravalli crests receive reduced settlement suitability, whereas alluvial terraces, interfluvial doabs and deltaic lowlands receive high base capacity weights.
3. Historical irrigation corridors and soil suitability: incorporating mapped channels of the Tughlaq canals, deep alluvial soils in the Indo-Gangetic basin and rich regur (black cotton soil) tracts in the Malwa and Deccan plateaus.
4. Commercial accessibility and trade thoroughfares: proximity to historical overland routes (including the ancient Uttarapatha connecting Peshawar to Sonargaon) and navigable riverine waterways.

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To prevent double counting between nucleated urban centres and surrounding agricultural cultivators, 34.677 catalogued settlements with active chronological population trajectories are anchored directly to their WGS84 coordinates. At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements inside each sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The remaining rural population is then allocated across non-settled grid cells in proportion to their environmental suitability scores. A two-pass boundary smoothing algorithm feathers density gradients across sub-regional borders, preventing artificial step discontinuities along administrative demarcations while respecting major physical barriers.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every sub-regional and macro-regional benchmark estimate carries an explicit uncertainty interval reflecting variations among historical demographic authorities [@Torri2014Periodizat; @Jayaneththi2025South; @Eaton2019India]. Early benchmarks (1206AD to 1450AD) maintain a symmetric uncertainty envelope of +/- 20%, accommodating diverse interpretations of pre-Mughal fiscal records and chroniclers' army counts.

By 1526AD, the uncertainty band tightens to +/- 14%, reflecting the closer proximity to late sixteenth-century Mughal revenue statistics documented in the Ain-i-Akbari and analysed by modern scholars such as Moreland, Habib, Moosvi and Lal [@Habib1982Atlas; @Moosvi1987Economy; @Torri2014Periodizat; @Lan2026Golden; @Akram2024Discourse]. In 1206AD, the regional total of 74M is bounded between 59,2M and 88,8M, while in 1526AD, the total of 97M is bounded between 83,4M and 110,6M inhabitants.

## Benchmark Population Dynamics

The aggregate demographic evolution of the subcontinent across the Sultanate era exhibits consistent, sustained growth punctuated by regional political realignments (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

<figure class="crd-table-figure" id="tab:benchmarks">

## Historical Demographic Phases

### Early Mamluk Consolidation and Khalji Centralisation (1206AD to 1320AD)

The first phase spans the foundation of the Sultanate under Qutb al-Din Aibak, Iltutmish and Balban, culminating in the centralised autocracy of Alauddin Khalji [@Aamir2026Slave; @Hannan2025Sufic; @Malik2026Trade]. Across these eleven decades, regional population expanded from 74M to 81M inhabitants, an aggregate increase of 9,46% at an annual growth rate of 0,082%.

Growth was propelled by the pacification of transit routes across the Doab, the suppression of dacoity and rural banditry in Mewat and Awadh, and the expansion of cultivated land surrounding garrison towns [@Amir2023Taking; @Rao2026Healing]. Balban cleared dense thickets surrounding Delhi, established permanent military cantonments in the Doab and erected roadside forts garrisoned by Afghan mercenaries [@Eaton2019India].

Alauddin Khalji's military campaigns successfully checked repeated Mongol invasions in the Punjab while subordinating the Yadavas of Devagiri, the Kakatiyas of Warangal, the Hoysalas of Dvarasamudra and the Pandyas of Madurai [@Eaton2019India; @Ali2023Historical]. The influx of tribute and captured bullion into Delhi spurred unprecedented monumental construction, including the fortified royal city of Siri and the monumental Alai Darwaza [@BurtonPage2008Documentat; @Mahata2024Distinctiv].

### Tughlaq Expansion, Hydraulic Canals and Disintegration (1320AD to 1398AD)

The second phase commenced with the founding of the Tughlaq dynasty by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq and reached peak territorial expanse under Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325AD-1351AD) [@BurtonPage2008Documentat; @Eaton2019India]. Under Muhammad bin Tughlaq, the Sultanate attempted the direct administrative absorption of peninsular India, temporarily relocating the administrative apparatus to Daulatabad (Devagiri) in Maharashtra to serve as a secondary imperial capital [@BurtonPage2008Documentat; @Torri2014Periodizat].

However, severe agrarian rebellions in the Doab precipitated by excessive tax assessments, compounded by regional revolts in Madurai, Bengal and the Deccan, undermined central control [@Eaton2019India]. Firoz Shah Tughlaq stabilised the northern core through agrarian concessions, debt forgiveness and his celebrated canal-building projects along the Yamuna and Ghaggar [@GANI2026Canal; @Khan2024Hydraulic]. Regional population increased from 81M in 1300AD to 83M in 1350AD and 86,5M by 1400AD.

Firoz Shah also created extensive state orchard and horticultural holdings around Delhi, numbering more than twelve hundred gardens, which yielded substantial non-tax revenues for the crown while supplying urban markets with fresh fruit and vegetables [@GANI2026Canal].

### Post-Timurid Fragmentation and Regional Sultanate Florescence (1398AD to 1480AD)

The devastating sack of Delhi by Timur in December 1398AD dealt a fatal blow to centralised imperial authority, triggering the rapid decentralisation of political and economic power [@Eaton2019India; @BurtonPage2008Documentat]. Rather than inducing general demographic decline, this political dissolution fostered an era of flourishing regional urbanisation [@Sheikh2004State; @Salim2026Social].

Wealth, artisanal talent and administrative expertise flowed outward to provincial capitals, which grew rapidly into autonomous urban centres:

1. In Jaunpur, the Sharqi sultans constructed the grand Atala and Jami mosques, making the city a renowned centre of scholarship celebrated as the Shiraz of India [@Joshi2026Sacred; @Kulke2009Bibliograp].
2. In Bengal, the restored Ilyas Shahi dynasty rebuilt Gaur and Pandua into magnificent brick metropolises, welcoming Chinese diplomatic missions and trading extensively across maritime Southeast Asia [@Salim2026Social; @Eaton2019India].
3. In Gujarat, Ahmad Shah I established Ahmedabad in 1411AD on the Sabarmati River, creating an international manufacturing centre for dyed cottons, silks and paper [@Sheikh2004State; @Sheikh2021Persian].
4. In Malwa, Sultan Hoshang Shah transformed Mandu into an impregnable hilltop palace city adorned with the Jahaz Mahal and marble mausoleums [@BurtonPage2008Documentat].
5. In the Deccan, the Bahmani court at Bidar erected the celebrated Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan, attracting scholars from across Iran, Central Asia and the Arab world [@BurtonPage2008Documentat; @Eaton2019India].

Between 1400AD and 1450AD, total population expanded from 86,5M to 91M, demonstrating the resilience of regional agrarian and commercial systems during imperial decentralisation.

### Lodi Ascendancy and Eve of the Mughal Conquest (1480AD to 1526AD)

The final phase witnessed the partial recentralisation of northern India under the Afghan Lodi dynasty (Bahlul Lodi, Sikandar Lodi and Ibrahim Lodi) [@Eaton2019India; @Akram2024Discourse]. Bahlul Lodi annexed the Jaunpur Sultanate in 1479AD, reintegrating the middle Gangetic plains into the Delhi sphere.

In 1504AD, Sikandar Lodi founded the new imperial capital of Agra on the Yamuna River, strategically positioning the court to supervise both the Doab and the rebellious marches of Rajputana [@BurtonPage2008Documentat]. Agra rapidly attracted merchants, scholars and soldiers, serving as the forward operational base for campaigns against Gwalior and Dholpur.

Under the Lodi sultans, demographic growth was further stimulated by the systematic settlement of Afghan military lineages (such as the Farmulis, Nohanis and Sarwanis) across Awadh, Bihar and the Doab [@Eaton2019India; @Akram2024Discourse]. Rather than ruling strictly as detached autocrats, the Lodi monarchs governed as primus inter pares among tribal sardars, parceling out extensive jagirs that encouraged Afghan kinsmen to migrate from Roh and the north-western highlands to colonise Gangetic agricultural tracts [@Akram2024Discourse]. These martial settlers founded fortified estate towns and sponsored irrigation wells, infusing new demographic energy into the rural economy on the eve of the Mughal era.

By 1526AD, total population reached 97M inhabitants. Across the subcontinent, expanding urban centres, flourishing port cities and highly commercialised agrarian networks created a wealthy, sophisticated economy that immediately attracted the attention of Zahir al-Din Muhammad Babur, whose victory over Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat on 21 April 1526 established the Mughal Empire [@Lan2026Golden; @Akram2024Discourse; @Banister2025Across].

# Urban Centres and Settlement Gazetteers

The INDUS gazetteer integrates 34.677 catalogued settlements across the subcontinent, detailing geographic coordinates, administrative affiliations and chronological population trajectories from 1206AD to 1526AD: 5.362 in the Delhi Core, Upper Doab, Awadh and Jaunpur division, 8.389 in Bengal, Bihar, Orissa and Assam, 5.708 in Gujarat, Malwa and Rajputana, 8.125 in the Bahmani and Deccan region, and 7.093 across Lahore, Multan and Sindh. Ranked by peak population, the urban hierarchy conforms closely to a Zipf rank-size distribution ($\alpha = 0,90$, $R^2 = 0,98$; Figure \ref{fig:trajectory}B). Table \ref{tab:leading_settlements} presents the leading urban settlements ordered by peak population.

Imperial Delhi occupied a pre-eminent position in the urban hierarchy of northern South Asia [@BurtonPage2008Documentat; @Mahata2024Distinctiv; @Hambly1982Towns]. Rather than a single contiguous city, mediaeval Delhi comprised a constellation of successive royal cities constructed across the rocky southern ridge of the Aravalli hills overlooking the Yamuna: Qila Rai Pithora around the Qutb Minar complex, Alauddin Khalji's circular fortress at Siri (1303AD), Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's massive cyclopean stone citadel at Tughlaqabad (1321AD), Muhammad bin Tughlaq's fortified enclosure at Jahanpanah (1326AD) and Firoz Shah Tughlaq's riverfront palace city at Firozabad (1354AD) [@BurtonPage2008Documentat; @Mahata2024Distinctiv; @Jha2025Geoarchaeo; @Blake1991Shahjahanabad]. Expanding from 130k residents in 1206AD to 260k in 1300AD, Delhi attained its Sultanate zenith of 340k inhabitants in 1350AD before Timur's 1398AD sack halved the city to 140k in 1400AD; subsequent recovery brought it to 170k in 1450AD, 185k in 1500AD and 165k in 1526AD.

Following its foundation by Sikandar Lodi in 1504AD, Agra expanded rapidly as a forward administrative and military capital, reaching 95k residents by 1526AD and laying the groundwork for its subsequent role as a Mughal imperial seat [@BurtonPage2008Documentat; @Naqvi1968Urbanisation]. Elsewhere in the upper and middle Gangetic zone, Jaunpur peaked at 110k residents in 1450AD (65k in 1526AD), Varanasi reached 105k inhabitants by 1526AD, and Srinagar in the Kashmir valley peaked at 95k in 1450AD (90k in 1526AD) [@Hambly1982Towns; @Bayly1983Rulers].

In Gujarat and Malwa, the urban hierarchy shifted from older Chaulukya seats towards fifteenth-century sultanate capitals [@Sheikh2004State; @Sheikh2021Persian]. Patan (Anhilwara) had peaked at 120k inhabitants in 1206AD before moderating to 45k by 1526AD, whereas Ahmedabad, founded in 1411AD, expanded steadily to reach 165k residents by 1526AD. Alongside Ahmedabad, the maritime emporium of Khambhat (Cambay) peaked at 105k inhabitants in 1450AD (95k in 1526AD), Champaner reached 75k by 1526AD, and Surat emerged after 1500AD as a rising coastal port of 35k residents in 1526AD.

In eastern India, the Bengal Sultanate capitals at Gaur (Lakhnauti) and Pandua formed massive brick urban complexes embedded in deltaic waterways [@Salim2026Social; @Eaton1993Rise; @Eaton2019India]. Pandua peaked at 135k inhabitants around 1400AD during the height of Ilyas Shahi patronage before contracting to 18k in 1526AD once the court returned permanently to Gaur, which expanded to 220k residents by 1526AD behind expansive earthen dykes and masonry gateways. Further east, the riverine emporium of Sonargaon reached 85k residents in 1526AD and Chittagong 48k, while upstream in Bihar the strategic river port of Patna maintained 48k inhabitants in 1526AD.

In the Deccan and peninsular South Asia, urban concentrations matched or surpassed those of the northern plains [@Eaton2019India; @Chatterjee2006Slavery; @Stein1989Vijayanagara; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade]. Along the Tungabhadra river, the imperial capital of the Vijayanagara Empire at Hampi expanded from 85k residents in 1350AD to 450k inhabitants in 1526AD, making it the largest urban agglomeration on the subcontinent. Within the Deccan polities, Daulatabad peaked at 117,1k inhabitants in 1350AD following Muhammad bin Tughlaq's southern capital experiment (55k in 1526AD), Bidar peaked at 110k in 1450AD (85k in 1526AD), Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) peaked at 95k in 1400AD (42k in 1526AD), Warangal peaked at 95k in 1300AD (35k in 1526AD), while Golconda (105k), Vijayapura (95k) and Ahmadnagar (75k) reached their regional maxima by 1526AD [@BurtonPage2008Documentat; @Eaton2019India].

In Malwa, the capital fortress of Mandu (Shadiabad) occupied a commanding plateau rising 634 metres above sea level, enclosed by 37 kilometres of stone curtain walls [@BurtonPage2008Documentat]. Mandu incorporated grand architectural ensembles such as the Jahaz Mahal, elevated between artificial lakes to catch prevailing breezes, alongside massive domed granaries and water-harvesting cisterns that sustained 110k inhabitants at its 1450AD peak (95k in 1526AD) [@BurtonPage2008Documentat].

In Jaunpur, the Sharqi capital along the Gomti River developed distinctive architectural innovations, notably the monumental pylon screens (*propylons*) of the Atala Mosque (completed 1408AD) and Jami Mosque [@BurtonPage2008Documentat; @Mahata2024Distinctiv]. These towering arched facades masked the central prayer halls while incorporating local trabeated stone carving, reflecting deep syncretism between Islamic structural forms and indigenous stone-crafting guilds [@Mahata2024Distinctiv].

Along the maritime littoral of western India, Khambhat (Cambay) served as the primary gateway for international oceanic trade, celebrated by Ibn Battuta for its handsome mansions, foreign merchant colonies and skilled lapidaries who cut agate and carnelian from the Ratanpur mines [@Sheikh2004State; @Sheikh2021Persian]. On the Coromandel coast, Machilipatnam (35k in 1526AD) acted as the principal maritime outlet for Golconda, exporting painted kalamkari textiles and diamonds to markets throughout the Indian Ocean [@Malik2026Trade], while on the Konkan coast Old Goa reached 65k inhabitants by 1526AD.

In eastern coastal Orissa, the Gajapati capital at Cuttack (82k in 1526AD) was anchored by the formidable Barabati fort, surrounded by a broad water moat excavated from the Kathajodi and Mahanadi river channels [@Kulke2009Bibliograp; @Jha2025Geoarchaeo]. South of Cuttack, the temple city of Puri (45k in 1526AD) developed an extensive urban precinct centred on the Jagannath temple complex, whose daily kitchen endowments (*mahaprasad*) fed thousands of resident priests, pilgrims and administrative retainers [@Kulke2009Bibliograp].

In the north-west, Thatta in lower Sindh and Lahore in the Punjab each reached 110k inhabitants by 1526AD, flanked by Multan (85k peak in 1350AD, 80k in 1526AD) and Peshawar (50k in 1526AD), anchoring caravan traffic crossing the Sulaiman ranges towards Kabul, Qandahar and Samarkand [@Ali2023Historical; @Malik2021Colonial]. At Thatta, the administrative capital of the Samma dynasty stood adjacent to the vast Makli necropolis spanning 10 km² and containing thousands of intricately carved sandstone tombs that blended Gujarati floral motifs with Persian tilework [@Ali2023Historical; @BurtonPage2008Documentat].

By georeferencing 34.677 catalogued settlements, INDUS balances nucleated urban centres against rural populations, demonstrating that late mediaeval India was a densely settled, technologically sophisticated and highly urbanised civilisation.
